Like chess, the goal is to capture the enemy king. Unlike chess, the identity of the king can strategically change. Each player starts with 8 pieces that can move 1 space in any direction. If pieces move onto empty spaces, they increase their move range, but all moves must be an exact distance. If pieces capture enemies, the capturing piece resets its range to 1. The identity of the king changes to whichever piece has the uniquely highest move range. Number of players: 2 Game duration: 4 mn Complexity: 2 / 5 Play Lielow and 1414 other games online. Discover Board Game Arena Rules summary Contents 1 Setup 2 Gameplay 3 Kings 4 End of Game Setup Each player has 8 pieces on a chess board. Each piece is level 1. Gameplay White plays first. Each turn, the player must move one piece an exact number of squares equal to the piece's level. Pieces can move horizontally, vertically, or diagonally. Pieces can move through all other pieces, but cannot land on friendly pieces. If a piece lands on an empty space, the piece gains 1 level. If a piece lands on an enemy piece, the enemy piece is removed from the game, and the moving piece resets to level 1. If a piece would move off the board, its level does not change, and it is removed from the game. Kings The identity of each player's king changes throughout the game according to the following rule: After each move, both players check the levels of their pieces. If a player has exactly one piece that is higher level than all others of that player, that piece becomes the player's king. There is no other way for their king's identity to change. Note that another of a player's pieces may gain a level and tie that player's king, but the king's identity does NOT change in this situation. End of Game You win if your piece lands on your opponent's king. You also win if your opponent chooses to move their king off the board. [Rating: 1/10] Abstract strategy, not my type. Some variant of King being behind, but still boring.

[Rating: 4/10] Capture games aren't my thing, though Lielow does have some interesting tricks up its sleeves. My favorite element is that your king can change during play. All-in-all, I thought Lielow was more an interesting design than a fun one. I'm not the target audience for this.  EDIT: Yeah, I'm too smooth-brained for this

[Rating: 5/10] I tend to dislike moving-piece abstracts. I know, that's ridiculous! What about chess? I don't like chess much either. I'm working on it.  At any rate, this spoke to me... a little bit. The movement rules make it much easier to see what's possible and what you might need to worry about, which in turn gives me a little insight into why chess and its relatives often don't land for me! I'm not sure I'll be playing more Lielow, but I will be thinking about it.

[Rating: 7/10] Clever game of manoeuvring checker pieces on a chess board to capture opponent's king.  The tricks are that the King can change (it's the highest numbered piece) and captures reduce values to 1.  Nice abstract.  I guess you could play this with dice or numbered counters.

[Rating: 7/10] Fast-playing capture game where moving a piece makes its next move bigger. Sudden changes in movement potential create interesting puzzles. Early gridlock, then escalating chaos.  Many early board states seem opaque, then something crystalizes and there’s a quick, straightforward endgame. Though I like short games, I do find myself wishing for a touch more legible cognitive crunch between these extremes.

[Rating: 8/10] A pretty interesting abstract game with lots of openness for interesting plays and outmaneuvering your opponent. I also like that the game does have an ending and can't end in a draw, even if it takes several turns to get there. Played only online, and it does seem like it would be difficult to actually play IRL.

[Rating: 8/10] Clever enjoyable little game of stacks jumping a distance equal to their height, so options reduce quickly. But a stack that captures another (by moving onto its space) is reduced to height 1 again, so capturing is doubly valuable (reduce enemy stacks, and increase your own mobility options & remaining time). Guaranteed to terminate since eventually you'll have to jump a stack off the board (suiciding it), if the game doesn't win by a king being captured first.  The migrating kingship (unique highest stack on a side becomes king, so usually your tallest stack is your king, but not necessarily)
